text:
Moth and Gravel, Field Note 14.
Enough light to read by. An AI

narrated edition of the
published note. The navigation

screen reads 0.0 knots. Above
the number, in smaller letters,

it says my star slash fixed
study slash no live voyage.

Beyond the wheelhouse windows,
it is night. The console lights

are low and the sea is moving.
Each of those things is true in

a different way. That difference
became the study. A bridge at

night is a reading room. A
ship's bridge after dark is a

strange place to design for. The
people in it need to see out.

The screens in front of them
want to be seen. Every lit pixel

competes with the water beyond
the glass. So the brightest

thing in the room is a decision.
Our wheelhouse has a dimmer. It

turns down the instrument faces
and the light they spill onto

the console together, the way a
real lamp would. The labels on

the desk stay engraved and
quiet. Nothing glows for

atmosphere. We wanted the
screens to give enough light to

read by and no more. That turned
out to be a useful brief for the

words on them, too. Three kinds
of true. The study holds a

passenger ferry at a fixed
position off Tallinn, with

Helsinki's West Terminal 2 and
Tallinn's D Terminal across the

water. It's weather is observed.
Cloud, visibility, wind and sea

come from the nearest Finnish
Meteorological Institute

stations, and the screen says
how far away each station is.

Sometimes that is 3 km,
sometimes it is nearly 70. It's

night can be depicted at any
hour. Set the clock to 1900

Coordinated Universal Time, and
the sun follows the date and the

place. It drops below the
horizon, the cabin windows and

quay lamps come up, and the
water picks up their

reflections. So a single frame
can hold three different kinds

of truth. The sky was observed
that morning some distance away.

The night is a lighting study
placed at an hour that had not

yet come. The ship has not moved
at all. None of that is a

problem until it is presented as
one thing. A finished, carefully

lit scene lends every part of it
the same confidence. The work

was making sure each part kept
its own.

What the screen says when it has
nothing to say. The navigation

and contact screens under
depicted night lighting, the

17th of October, with that
morning's weather retained.

Actual study capture. The local
recording control is visible at

lower right. Watch the bridge
films. A fixed study is a

convenient place to work.
Nothing has to arrive before you

can look at hull lines, harbor
lights or a console at night. It

is also an easy place to start
lying because nothing arrives to

contradict you. So the
instruments name the study

before they give a number. Speed
over ground, 0.0 knots, because

the ship is held still. Depth,
rudder and radar, a dash labeled

as unavailable on-board inputs.
Contacts, no nearby AIS reports

received and no synthetic
contacts added to fill the

screen. A plausible depth would
have looked more finished. A few

drifting vessels would have made
the contact list feel alive. The

dash is less handsome and more
accurate. Where the study has no

source, it shows the absence
plainly. Fixed is not the same

as frozen. A fixed position does
not make a still picture. The

sea keeps moving, shaped by
observed wind and wave

measurements where a nearby
station reports them. Fields

that are missing fall back to
visual defaults and the study

says so, rather than quietly
filling them in. Night works the

same way. When we move the clock
forward, the weather stays as it

was observed and the screen says
that too. A lighting study must

not become a forecast by
accident. The harbors have the

same honesty problem in brick
and glass. Footprints and roads

come from OpenStreetMap. The two
terminals are shaped from

published architectural
references, then simplified for

the distance you see them from.
It is a harbor at viewing scale,

not a survey. Built on our own
ground. All of this sits on

Rivary, the framework we build
our own work on. It is a

full-stack TypeScript framework
for Bun. Server functions

without the usual plumbing with
CBOR O on the wire. Typed REST

endpoints, a small pure
functional PostgreSQL query

builder, streaming and caching,
and orchestration for AI agents.

The maritime study uses a modest
slice of it. Bun bundles the

scene and serves two harbor
weather endpoints. React 19 and

3js draw the ship, the harbors
and the wheelhouse. The ship,

the console and the camera are
shared components. So a change

to how the bridge is inspected
reaches every view that uses

them. That is the quiet benefit
of owning the ground you stand

on. The labels, the dashes and
the rules about what may be

shown live in the same place as
the hull and the lamps. Rivary

is private for now. We can
describe it. Its code stays in

the workshop. What we have not
shown. We have not put this

bridge in front of someone who
stands a watch for a living.

That is the next honest test.
Show them the night console

without explanation and ask what
the ship is doing and how they

know. If they read a fixed study
as a crossing, the labels still

have work to do. If they find
the dash before the number, the

screen is doing its job. Until
then, it is a quiet room with

the lights turned down. Enough
light to read by. Enough words

to know what you are reading.
Study scope. Visualization, not

navigation. These captures
contain this note accompanies

the maritime study specimen.
Positions are fixed, no voyage

is shown. Weather and sea come
from nearby FMI observations

where available, with visual
defaults for missing fields. The

night captures are a lighting
study, not a forecast. Harbor

architecture is reference
informed and simplified. The

ferry is drawn from published
dimensions. Nothing here comes

from aboard the ship or from its
operator. It is a visualization

study, not a navigational tool,
and it makes no safety or

compliance claim. The
application source is private.

No reader comprehension result
is established. Weather
observations, FMI CCBY 4.0.

Map data, copyright
OpenStreetMap contributors,

ODBL. Basemap, Natural Earth,
public domain. Inspect the

captures and working record.
Read the source and media
provenance.
